questions.title: What a DFD shows
questions.text: What does a **data flow diagram (DFD)** show?

options.content: The order in which the steps of an algorithm are carried out
How data moves through a system: its inputs, processes, data stores and outputs
The tables of a database and the relationships between them
The hardware devices of a computer network

questions.title: Outputs of a system
questions.text:
*A hotel booking system: a guest sends a booking request and a payment; the system reads room details from D1 Rooms, sends the guest a booking confirmation and an invoice, and sends housekeeping a daily cleaning list.*

Select the **three** data flows that are **outputs** of the system.

*Library level-1 DFD: the librarian enters new book details, which process 1 Register book saves as a book record in D1 Books. It may add a new external entity, Receptionist, that was not on the context diagram
It shows no external entities, only processes and data stores
It must show exactly three processes, one for each entity

scheme.mark_scheme: A

questions.title: Allowed flows
questions.text: Tick (✓) to show whether each data flow is **allowed** in a DFD.

scheme.mark_scheme: Customer → Process: allowed (1); Customer → Data store: not allowed (1); Process → Data store: allowed (1); Data store → Data store: not allowed (1); Customer → Supplier: not allowed (1)
scheme.ai_instructions: Award 4 for five correct, 3 for four, 2 for three, 1 for one or two.
scheme.explanation: Every flow must start or end at a process. Entity → store, store → store and entity → entity flows are not allowed.

questions.title: The rule behind the flows
questions.text:
Complete the rule.

Every data flow in a DFD must start or end at a [[1]]. So data cannot go directly from an external entity to a data [[2]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) process (2) store

questions.title: Why the flow is wrong
questions.text: Why is an arrow from the external entity **Student** directly to the data store **D2 Students** not allowed?

options.content: Data can only be stored by a process, so the data must pass through a process first
Data stores can only send data, never receive it
The arrow must always point from the store to the entity

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: Correcting an illegal flow
questions.text: A DFD has an arrow labelled *customer details* going directly from **Customer** to **D1 Customers**. What is the best correction?

options.content: Reverse the arrow so it goes from D1 Customers to Customer
Add a process such as *1 Register customer* between Customer and D1 Customers
Remove the label from the arrow
Change D1 Customers into an external entity

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Only a process can write to a data store: Customer → 1 Register customer → D1 Customers.

questions.title: Writing and reading stores
questions.text: In a complete DFD, every data store is written to by at least one process and read by at least one process.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: A store that is never written to has no data; a store that is never read is useless.

questions.title: Process numbers
questions.text: The numbers 1, 2, 3 on the processes of a DFD show the order in which the processes happen.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: The numbers only identify the processes; a DFD does not show order.

questions.title: A process with no output
questions.text: Process **3 Produce report** in a DFD has two input flows and **no** output flows. What is this error called?

questions.title: DFD errors
questions.text: Match each DFD error to its description.

right.text: A process has outputs but no input
An arrow goes from an external entity straight to a data store
A process has inputs but no output
The outputs cannot be produced from the inputs

scheme.mark_scheme: Black hole – A process has inputs but no output; Miracle – A process has outputs but no input; Grey hole – The outputs cannot be produced from the inputs; Illegal flow – An arrow goes from an external entity straight to a data store. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Find the illegal flows
questions.text: A student drew a DFD for a gym. Select the **three** flows that **break** the rules of DFDs.

scheme.mark_scheme: B and C and E. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Spot the data store
questions.text:
*"A receptionist enters each new patient's details, which are saved in the patient file. The system then books an appointment and sends the patient a confirmation."*

Which of these should be drawn as a **data store**?

questions.text:
Complete the method.

First underline the external [[1]] in the description. The processes are usually the [[2]] in the description. Data that the system must keep becomes a data [[3]]. Finally check that the level-1 DFD is [[4]] with the context diagram.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) entities / entity (2) verbs / verb / actions (3) store / stores (4) balanced / consistent

questions.text: A DFD shows the order in which the processes are carried out and the decisions between them.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Order and decisions are shown in a flowchart; a DFD shows only the movement of data.

questions.title: DFD, flowchart, ERD
questions.text: Match each diagram to what it shows.

right.text: The entities of a database and the relationships between them
How data moves between entities, processes and data stores
The sequence of steps and decisions in an algorithm

questions.text: Each data store in a DFD usually becomes a table (entity) when the database is designed in the ERD.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.

questions.title: Advantages of DFDs
questions.text: Select the **two** advantages of using DFDs when designing a new system.

options.content: The simple symbols can be understood and checked by the client
They show the inputs, outputs and storage of the whole system on one page
They show the order in which every step is carried out
They show how the algorithm inside each process works

questions.title: Driving school booking system
questions.text: **AltynDrive** is a driving school in Karaganda. Learners book driving lessons online. The system checks the instructors' free times in the *Instructors* file, saves each booking in the *Bookings* file and sends the learner a booking confirmation. Learners pay by card; the bank sends a payment confirmation. Every evening each instructor receives a timetable for the next day.

parts.title: Purpose of a DFD
parts.text: State the purpose of a data flow diagram.

scheme.mark_scheme: - shows how data moves through the system / its inputs, processes, data stores and outputs (1)

points.criterion: How data flows through the system (inputs, processes, stores, outputs)

scheme.model_answer: A DFD shows how data flows through the system — where it comes from, how it is processed, where it is stored and where it goes.

parts.title: Classify DFD elements
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show how each item would appear in a DFD of the AltynDrive system.

scheme.mark_scheme: Instructor – External entity (1); Bookings – Data store (1); Check free times – Process (1); booking confirmation – Data flow (1)
scheme.model_answer: Instructor: External entity; Bookings: Data store; Check free times: Process; booking confirmation: Data flow.

parts.title: Context diagram
parts.text: Draw a **context diagram** for the AltynDrive system.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- one process for the whole system, e.g. 0 Booking system, and no data stores (1)
- external entities Learner, Bank, Instructor (1)
- inputs: lesson request / booking details and card details from Learner; payment confirmation from Bank (1)
- outputs: booking confirmation to Learner, payment request to Bank, timetable to Instructor; all flows labelled (1)

- data stores are inside the system, so they appear only when the system is split into its main processes at level 1 (1)

scheme.model_answer: The context diagram shows the whole system as a single process with only the external entities around it. The Bookings file is inside the system, so it only appears on the level-1 DFD, where the system is split into processes that read and write the stores.

questions.title: Errors in a cinema DFD
questions.text:
A student drew a level-1 DFD for the **KinoPark** cinema booking system. These are some of its data flows:

| From | Data flow | To |
|---|---|---|
| Customer | seat request | D1 Seats |
| D1 Seats | free seats | 1 Book seat |
| 1 Book seat | booking | D2 Bookings |
| D2 Bookings | booking list | D3 Shows |
| Customer | review | Manager |

Process **2 Print ticket** has an output *ticket* to the Customer but **no input**.

parts.text: Identify **two** data flows in the table that break the rules of DFDs. For each one, explain why it is not allowed.

parts.title: Name the error

questions.title: Pharmacy order system
questions.text:
**DariHouse** is a pharmacy chain. A new system is being designed:

*A customer sends an order for medicines. The system checks the price and stock of each medicine in the Medicines file and saves the order in the Orders file. The customer receives an invoice. A pharmacist reads the new orders from the Orders file through the system and receives a packing list. When stock of a medicine is low, the system sends a re-order request to the supplier and updates the Medicines file when the supplier sends a delivery note.*

parts.title: Identify the elements
parts.text: Identify **two** external entities, **two** processes and **two** data stores for a level-1 DFD of this system.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- two external entities: Customer, Pharmacist, Supplier (1)
- two processes with verb + noun names, e.g. Take order, Produce packing list, Re-order stock, Record delivery (1)
- two data stores: D1 Medicines, D2 Orders (1)
scheme.model_answer: Entities: Customer, Supplier. Processes: 1 Take order, 3 Re-order stock. Data stores: D1 Medicines, D2 Orders.

parts.title: Draw the level-1 DFD
parts.text: Draw a **first-level DFD** for the DariHouse system. Show input, processing, storage and output.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- at least three processes with verb + noun names, e.g. Take order, Produce packing list, Re-order stock / Record delivery (1)
- data stores D1 Medicines and D2 Orders (1)
- input order from Customer and output invoice to Customer (1)
- output packing list to Pharmacist (1)
- re-order request to Supplier and delivery note from Supplier, with D1 Medicines updated (1)
- store flows correct (Medicines read for price / stock; order written to Orders and read for packing list); every flow labelled; no entity–store, store–store or entity–entity flows (1)

points.criterion: At least three processes, verb + noun
Store flows correct, labelled, no illegal flows

scheme.model_answer: Customer —order→ 1 Take order; D1 Medicines —price, stock→ 1; 1 —order record→ D2 Orders; 1 —invoice→ Customer. D2 Orders —new orders→ 2 Produce packing list —packing list→ Pharmacist. D1 Medicines —low stock data→ 3 Re-order stock —re-order request→ Supplier. Supplier —delivery note→ 4 Record delivery —updated stock→ D1 Medicines.
scheme.ai_instructions: Accept equivalent process names and different splits of the processes. Do not award the last point if there is any entity–store, store–store or entity–entity flow or an unlabelled flow.

parts.title: Input and output
parts.text: Identify **one** input to the system and **one** output from the system. Give the name of the data flow and the external entity for each.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- input: order from Customer / delivery note from Supplier (1)
- output: invoice to Customer / packing list to Pharmacist / re-order request to Supplier (1)
scheme.model_answer: Input: *order* from the Customer. Output: *packing list* to the Pharmacist.

parts.title: Balancing
parts.text: The analyst also drew a context diagram for this system. Explain what it means for the level-1 DFD to be **balanced** with the context diagram.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the level-1 DFD has the same external entities as the context diagram (1)
- and the same data flows into and out of the system / only detail inside the system is added (1)

points.criterion: Same flows in and out of the system

scheme.model_answer: Balanced means the level-1 DFD shows the same external entities (Customer, Pharmacist, Supplier) and the same data flows into and out of the system as the context diagram; it only adds processes and stores inside the system.

questions.title: DFDs and other design diagrams
questions.text: The analyst for DariHouse will hand the design to the programmers. The design contains a DFD, flowcharts and an ERD.

parts.title: DFD and flowchart
parts.text: Describe **two** differences between a data flow diagram and a flowchart.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two differences, 2 marks each (1 for the DFD side, 1 for the flowchart side):
- DFD shows the movement of data / flowchart shows the sequence of steps (1+1)
- DFD shows no decisions or loops / flowchart shows decisions and loops (1+1)
- DFD describes the whole system / flowchart describes one process or algorithm (1+1)
- DFD shows data stores and external entities / flowchart shows start/stop, input/output and process boxes (1+1)
scheme.model_answer: A DFD shows how data moves between entities, processes and stores, whereas a flowchart shows the sequence of steps. A DFD has no decisions or loops, whereas a flowchart shows decisions (diamonds) and loops.

parts.title: Why DFDs help the client
parts.text: Explain **one** reason why the analyst shows the DFD to the pharmacy's managers before the system is built.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- DFDs use a few simple symbols that non-technical people can understand (1)
- so the managers can check that all inputs / outputs / stored data are correct and nothing is missing before development, which is cheaper to fix now (1)

points.criterion: Client can check / correct requirements early

scheme.model_answer: The DFD uses only four simple symbols, so the managers can understand it and check that every input, output and stored item is correct before programming starts, when mistakes are cheap to fix.

parts.title: A limitation
parts.text: Explain **one** limitation of a DFD for the programmers.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- a DFD does not show how a process works / the algorithm / the order and decisions (1)
- so programmers need extra designs such as flowcharts or pseudocode for each process (1)
scheme.model_answer: A DFD does not show how each process works or the order of the steps, so the programmers also need a flowchart or pseudocode for each process.

summary: Data flow diagrams (DFDs) — what they show, the four symbols (external entity, process, data store, data flow), context diagrams and first-level DFDs, the rules for drawing them correctly, and how to create a level-1 DFD that shows input, processing, storage and output.

theory.title: What a data flow diagram shows

blocks.content: A diagram that shows **how data moves through a system**: where it comes **from** (inputs), how it is **processed**, where it is **stored**, and where it goes **to** (outputs). It shows **what** happens to the data, not **how** the program does it and not the **order** of events.

A DFD is drawn during **analysis** (to describe the current system) and **design** (to plan the new system). It helps the analyst, the programmers and the client agree on the **inputs, processes, outputs and storage (IPOS)** of the system before any code is written. A DFD uses only **four symbols**.

A person, organisation or other system **outside** the system being designed that **sends data into** the system (a **source**) or **receives data from** it (a **sink**). Named with a **noun**: *Customer*, *Bank*, *Teacher*.
An action **inside** the system that **transforms input data into output data**. It has a **number** and a **verb + noun** name: *1 Record order*, *2 Calculate bill*.
Data that is **held** in the system for later use — a file, a database table, a folder of forms. It has an **ID** (D1, D2…) and a **noun** name: *D1 Orders*.
**Data moving** from one symbol to another, drawn as an **arrow** that shows the direction and is labelled with the **name of the data** (a noun): *order details*, *payment*, *receipt*.

blocks.title: Different notations
blocks.content: This platform uses **Gane–Sarson** notation. Some books draw **processes as circles** (Yourdon–DeMarco notation) and data stores as two parallel lines. Any notation is accepted in the exam if it is **used consistently** and the four symbols are clearly different.
Entities and stores are **nouns**, processes are **verb + noun**, data flows are **nouns** that name the data — never "send", "check" or "go" on an arrow.

A DFD that shows the **whole system as one single process** with all the **external entities** and the data flows between them and the system. It shows the **boundary** of the system; it has **no data stores**.
A DFD that **splits the single process of the context diagram into its main processes** (usually 3–7), and shows the **data stores** and all the data flows between entities, processes and stores.

blocks.title: Data flows of the library level-1 DFD

blocks.content: A level-1 DFD is **balanced** with its context diagram when it has the **same external entities** and the **same data flows into and out of the system**. The level-1 diagram only adds detail **inside** the boundary.

blocks.title: Worked example — from context diagram to level 1 (school canteen)
blocks.content:
*The canteen system receives pre-orders from students, takes card payments through the bank and sends a daily list to the kitchen.*

1. **Context diagram:** one process *0 Canteen system*; entities **Student**, **Bank**, **Kitchen**; flows *meal choice*, *card details* in from Student; *order number* out to Student; *payment request* to Bank, *payment confirmation* from Bank; *meal list* to Kitchen.
2. **Main processes** (verbs in the description): *1 Take pre-order*, *2 Take payment*, *3 Print kitchen list*.
3. **Data stores** (what must be kept between processes): *D1 Pre-orders*, *D2 Menu*.
4. **Connect:** every context-diagram flow now goes to or from **one of the processes**; new flows appear only between processes and stores (e.g. *order record* 1 → D1, *prices* D2 → 1).
5. **Check balance:** the same 3 entities and the same 6 external flows appear on both diagrams. ✔

blocks.title: How to draw a context diagram
items: Draw **one process** in the middle and name it after the whole system: *0 Library system*.
Find every **external entity** — who gives data to the system or gets data from it.
Draw one **labelled arrow** for each kind of data going in or out.
Check: **no data stores**, no flows between two entities, every arrow touches the system.

theory.title: Exam practice: DFD symbols and levels

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: State the purpose of a data flow diagram. [1]**
To show **how data flows through a system** — its inputs, processes, outputs and data stores (1).

**Q: Describe what is represented by an external entity in a DFD. [2]**
A person / organisation / system **outside the system** (1) that **sends data to** or **receives data from** the system (1).

**Q: Give two differences between a context diagram and a level-1 DFD. [2]**
A context diagram shows the system as **one process**, a level-1 DFD shows the **main processes** (1). A context diagram has **no data stores**, a level-1 DFD **shows the data stores** (1).

**Q: In the library DFD, identify one input, one data store and one output. [3]**
Input: *student card, book ID* / *new book details* / *returned book ID* (1). Data store: *D1 Books* / *D2 Students* / *D3 Loans* (1). Output: *loan receipt* / *fine notice* / *overdue report* (1).

**Q: Explain why a context diagram has no data stores. [2]**
It shows the whole system as **one process / a black box** (1); data stores are **inside the system**, so they only appear when the system is split into processes in the level-1 DFD (1).

- Drawing a **data store on a context diagram** — stores appear only from level 1.
- Naming a process with a noun only ("Orders") — a process needs a **verb**: *Record order*.
- Naming a flow with an action ("check", "send") instead of the **data** ("order details").
- Drawing the **computer** or the **database** as an external entity — they are part of the system.
- A level-1 DFD with an entity or flow that is **not on the context diagram** (not balanced).

items.title: Rules for processes
items.content:
- Every process needs **at least one input and at least one output**.
- Name it **verb + noun**: *Validate payment*, *Calculate grade*.
- Number processes **1, 2, 3 …** — the numbers identify them, they do **not** show the order.

items.title: Rules for data stores
items.content:
- A data store is **written to** by at least one process and **read from** by at least one process.
- Give it an ID (**D1**) and a noun name; it can be drawn twice to avoid crossing lines.

items.title: Rules for flows
items.content:
- Every flow has a **name** — the data, a **noun** ("payment details").
- An arrow shows **one direction**; draw two arrows for data going both ways.
- Do not draw **decisions, loops or control signals** — a DFD is **not** a flowchart.

blocks.title: Common process errors
rows: "1 Record order" receives *order details* but sends nothing anywhere
Add the missing output, e.g. *order record* → D1 Orders
"2 Print invoice" produces an *invoice* from nothing
Add the input it needs, e.g. *order data* from D1 Orders
The outputs **cannot be produced** from the inputs
"3 Calculate total" receives only the customer's *name*
Add the data needed, e.g. *prices* from D2 Products

blocks.title: Worked example — find four errors in a gym DFD
blocks.content:
*A student's DFD for a gym: Member → D1 Members (membership form); 1 Book class → Trainer (class list); D2 Classes → D1 Members (class details); 2 Calculate fee has an input "member details" and no output; a flow from Member to Trainer called "question".*

| Error | Why it is wrong | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| Member → D1 Members | An **entity cannot write to a store** | Add *3 Register member*: Member → 3 → D1 Members |
| 1 Book class has no input | A **miracle** — the class list comes from nothing | Add *booking request* from Member and *class details* from D2 Classes |
| D2 Classes → D1 Members | **Store to store** is not allowed | Remove it, or move the data through a process |
| 2 Calculate fee has no output | A **black hole** | Add *fee* → Member (or *fee record* → D1 Members) |
| Member → Trainer "question" | **Entity to entity** is outside the system | Remove it |

- Joining an **entity directly to a data store**, or two stores together.
- **Unlabelled arrows**, or labels that are actions ("check") instead of data ("order details").
- Processes with **only inputs** (black hole) or **only outputs** (miracle).
- Thinking process numbers show the **order** — they are only identifiers.

theory.title: Creating a first-level DFD from a description

blocks.title: How to draw a level-1 DFD
items: Read the description and **underline the external entities** (who gives or receives data).
Find the **main processes** — the actions the system performs (verbs): *takes orders*, *checks stock*, *sends invoices*.
Find the **data stores** — data that is **kept** (customers, products, orders).
For each process list its **inputs** and **outputs** and where they come from / go to.
Draw the symbols, connect them with **named arrows**, and **check the rules** (no entity–store links, every process has input and output).
Check that the diagram is **balanced** with the context diagram.

items.title: Tips for a neat diagram
items.content:
- Put **entities at the edges**, **processes in the middle**, **stores** between the processes that share them.
- **Draw an entity or store twice** (with a mark) instead of crossing many lines.
- Use **two separate arrows** for data going in opposite directions.

items.title: What examiners give marks for
items.content:
- Correct **entities** and **data stores** taken from the scenario.
- **Processes** with verb + noun names that match the scenario.
- **Labelled flows** in the correct direction — inputs, outputs, reads and writes.
- **No rule-breaking** flows; nothing important from the scenario missed.

blocks.title: Drawing DFDs on the platform
blocks.content: In DFD questions, add **external entities**, **processes** and **data stores** from the toolbar, connect them by dragging between the dots, then **select each arrow** and type the name of the data flow.

blocks.title: DFD vs flowchart vs ERD
rows: **Movement of data** between entities, processes and stores
The **sequence of steps** and decisions in an algorithm
Each **data store** becomes a table in the ERD
Each **process** can be designed as a flowchart
Each **entity** usually matches a data store

blocks.title: Advantages and limitations of DFDs
rows: Simple symbols — the **client** can understand and check them
Do **not show the order** of processing or decisions
Show the **inputs, outputs and storage** of the whole system on one page
Do not show **how** a process works (needs a flowchart / pseudocode)
Make **missing data** and duplicated work easy to spot
Large systems need **many levels** of diagrams
Levels let the analyst move from **overview to detail**
Do not show timing or **who** does the work inside the system

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Identify one error in a DFD where the arrow goes directly from "Customer" to "D1 Customers". [2]**
An **external entity cannot send data directly to a data store** (1); the data must pass through a **process**, e.g. "1 Register customer" (1).

**Q: A process "3 Produce report" has two inputs and no outputs. Name this error and explain how to correct it. [2]**
A **black hole** (1); add an output flow, e.g. *report* to the Manager (1).

**Q: Explain why process numbers in a DFD do not show the order of processing. [2]**
A DFD shows the **movement of data**, not the **sequence** of steps (1); the numbers are only **identifiers** used to refer to processes / their level-2 diagrams (1).

**Q: Describe one difference between a DFD and a flowchart. [2]**
A DFD shows **how data moves** between entities, processes and stores (1); a flowchart shows the **sequence of steps and decisions** of an algorithm (1).

**Q: Draw a first-level DFD for the system described. [6]**
Credit is given for: correct **external entities**; correct **processes** with verb + noun names; correct **data stores**; **named data flows** in the correct directions; **no rule-breaking** flows; a diagram that matches the description.

- Joining an **entity directly to a data store**, or two stores together.
- **Unlabelled arrows**, or labels that are actions ("check") instead of data ("order details").
- Processes with **only inputs** (black hole) or **only outputs** (miracle).
- Including the **database or the computer** as an external entity.
- Drawing **decisions and loops** as in a flowchart.
- Missing a store that the scenario says is **kept** ("the details are saved…").
